query: In SEM-EDS / EPMA microanalysis, MgO (periclase) is used as a standard for Mg and O. If the MgO standard must be carbon-coated for conductivity: (1) does the coating itself add a C K-alpha peak to every spectrum, making a coated sample unusable as a carbon standard or for measuring sample carbon? (2) Roughly how much are O K-alpha (0.525 keV) and Mg K-alpha (1.254 keV) intensities attenuated by a 10-25 nm evaporated carbon coat at a 35-40 degree take-off angle? (3) What is best practice when the standard is coated but the unknowns are uncoated conductive metals - match the coating, or correct for it in software such as NIST DTSA-II?

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific

and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific

Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'armstrong2009useofmultilayer pages 1-2'.

J. Armstrong. Use of multilayer correction procedures to improve the quantitative electron microprobe analyses of coated insulating specimens. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 15:514-515, Jul 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927609098857, doi:10.1017/s1431927609098857. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt establishes that conductive surface coatings alter measured X-ray intensities and therefore must be included in quantitative EPMA corrections. It explicitly documents carbon analysis as a means of determining carbon-coat thickness, showing that the coating can contribute a measurable C signal; however, it does not provide a general quantitative discussion of characteristic X-ray production from every possible coating. Coatings also modify X-ray generation and transmission: correction requires accounting for electron energy losses and changes in direction within the overlayer, as well as X-ray absorption and fluorescence by the layer(s). The excerpt implies that these effects depend on coating composition and thickness, while the cited experimental context concerns emitted intensities and absorption; take-off-angle dependence is not explicitly stated in this passage. Best practice is to coat samples and standards simultaneously to obtain equal overlayer thickness, or use thickness monitors. If coatings differ in material or thickness, uncorrected errors may exceed 5–10%. Armstrong reports using multilayer algorithmic corrections (GMRFilm and CITZAF) and Monte Carlo simulations (CASINO), with strong results for differing carbon coats: Fe-oxide totals improved from 92–95% to 99.5–100.5%. Heavy-metal coatings, such as Pt, remained more model-dependent, although Monte Carlo results were promising.

From text 'ohfuji2015edsquantificationof pages 1-2'.

Hiroaki OHFUJI and Masashi YAMAMOTO. Eds quantification of light elements using osmium surface coating. Journal of Mineralogical and Petrological Sciences, 110:189-195, Jan 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.2465/jmps.141126, doi:10.2465/jmps.141126. This article has 30 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt emphasizes that conductive coatings can materially affect quantitative EPMA/EDS, especially for light-element analysis. It does not explicitly state that carbon or another coating contributes its own characteristic X-ray signal; instead, it focuses on the coating’s absorption/attenuation of X-rays and on selecting the coating material in the correction model. Low-energy characteristic X-rays, such as those used for oxygen, are particularly vulnerable to attenuation. The magnitude of the effect depends strongly on coating thickness: the study used a 5 nm osmium film, whereas the comparison carbon films were estimated at 15–20 nm. Osmium’s thinness and reproducibility allowed its thickness to be evaluated and absorption corrections to be applied precisely. In contrast, uncertainty in carbon-film thickness was associated with oxygen concentrations several wt% below stoichiometric values. The excerpt also warns that high-attenuation coatings such as gold and platinum are generally unsuitable for quantitative work and that coating choice can influence accuracy. The software correction described requires specifying the coating element and thickness. However, this passage does not discuss take-off-angle dependence, standards and unknowns having different coatings, explicit coating-generated characteristic peaks, or multilayer coating corrections. Those practices therefore cannot be established from this excerpt alone.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'ohfuji2015edsquantificationof pages 3-5'.

Hiroaki OHFUJI and Masashi YAMAMOTO. Eds quantification of light elements using osmium surface coating. Journal of Mineralogical and Petrological Sciences, 110:189-195, Jan 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.2465/jmps.141126, doi:10.2465/jmps.141126. This article has 30 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly addresses coating effects on low-energy X-ray quantification. It reports that a 5 nm osmium coating attenuates X-rays by approximately 11%, whereas a 15–20 nm carbon coating attenuates them by about 4–6%. Oxygen is particularly affected because its characteristic X-ray has lower energy than those of the other elements. Consequently, uncertainty in coating thickness produces a significant quantitative error: an error of ±5 nm in carbon-coating thickness gives an uncertainty of approximately 1.7% in the measured oxygen concentration. The authors emphasize that attenuation can be corrected if the actual coating thickness is supplied to the software, but fixed or default thickness values can cause non-negligible errors. Osmium is presented as advantageous because its plasma-CVD thickness is reproducible and controllable through coating time, discharge current, and pressure. The passage also notes that coating composition can contribute interfering characteristic radiation: gold is unsuitable for precise carbon analysis because gold’s N-fluorescent X-rays overlap the carbon K line at 0.277 keV. This excerpt does not explicitly discuss take-off-angle dependence, standards and unknowns having different coatings, or multilayer-coating correction procedures.

The excerpt states that conductive or contaminant surface layers can affect low-keV EPMA. Plasma cleaning, oil-free pumps, a cold plate, and thin Ir coatings were used to limit carbon-bearing contamination, but such films were not completely prevented. The resulting hydrocarbon or carbon films can contribute a carbon X-ray signal; treating this carbon as uniformly distributed in the interaction volume produces an overestimate when it actually occurs in localized contamination spots. Carbon also absorbs X-rays from other elements, so an incorrect carbon estimate propagates into the calculated concentrations of Fe, Si, Ni, and other elements. For quantitative work, the excerpt recommends correcting for the surface film rather than simply ignoring carbon. STRATAGem can compare measured k-ratios with X-ray generation and absorption models, represent one or more layers above the sample, and model carbon either in the substrate or in a surface film. The table illustrates that modeling carbon in the film produced EPMA results close to APT results. At low accelerating voltage, standards should be carefully matched to unknowns, or suitable nonstandard lines should be used, because chemical shifts, self-absorption, cross-section changes, and absorption-edge effects become important. The excerpt directly supports the importance of accounting for carbonaceous surface films in electron-probe analysis. Electron-beam exposure can produce a contamination layer, mainly carbon, from pump oil or hydrocarbons. This layer contributes its own carbon X-ray signal by enhancing C Ka intensity and simultaneously reduces the intensities of other X-ray lines through absorption. The passage therefore indicates that a coating can both generate a characteristic signal and attenuate signals originating from the specimen. It recommends keeping samples clean, storing them under vacuum where possible, using an oil trap, and employing a liquid-nitrogen cold finger or gas jet to prevent or remove contamination. The excerpt does not specifically quantify attenuation as a function of coating thickness or take-off angle, nor does it discuss a formal multilayer correction algorithm. For quantitative EPMA, it emphasizes using strong, stable, reproducible, homogeneous, independently characterized standards and selecting standards similar in composition and structure to the unknown. Such matching is intended to minimize matrix effects and spectral differences, including peak shifts and shape changes. By implication, standards and unknowns should have comparable surface conditions; otherwise, coating-related signal enhancement and absorption can bias quantitative results.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.

Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:

From text 'armstrong2009useofmultilayer pages 1-2'.

J. Armstrong. Use of multilayer correction procedures to improve the quantitative electron microprobe analyses of coated insulating specimens. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 15:514-515, Jul 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1017/s1431927609098857, doi:10.1017/s1431927609098857. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt establishes that conductive surface coatings alter measured X-ray intensities and therefore must be included in quantitative EPMA corrections. It explicitly documents carbon analysis as a means of determining carbon-coat thickness, showing that the coating can contribute a measurable C signal; however, it does not provide a general quantitative discussion of characteristic X-ray production from every possible coating. Coatings also modify X-ray generation and transmission: correction requires accounting for electron energy losses and changes in direction within the overlayer, as well as X-ray absorption and fluorescence by the layer(s). The excerpt implies that these effects depend on coating composition and thickness, while the cited experimental context concerns emitted intensities and absorption; take-off-angle dependence is not explicitly stated in this passage. Best practice is to coat samples and standards simultaneously to obtain equal overlayer thickness, or use thickness monitors. If coatings differ in material or thickness, uncorrected errors may exceed 5–10%. Armstrong reports using multilayer algorithmic corrections (GMRFilm and CITZAF) and Monte Carlo simulations (CASINO), with strong results for differing carbon coats: Fe-oxide totals improved from 92–95% to 99.5–100.5%. Heavy-metal coatings, such as Pt, remained more model-dependent, although Monte Carlo results were promising.

The excerpt emphasizes that conductive coatings can materially affect quantitative EPMA/EDS, especially for light-element analysis. It does not explicitly state that carbon or another coating contributes its own characteristic X-ray signal; instead, it focuses on the coating’s absorption/attenuation of X-rays and on selecting the coating material in the correction model. Low-energy characteristic X-rays, such as those used for oxygen, are particularly vulnerable to attenuation. The magnitude of the effect depends strongly on coating thickness: the study used a 5 nm osmium film, whereas the comparison carbon films were estimated at 15–20 nm. Osmium’s thinness and reproducibility allowed its thickness to be evaluated and absorption corrections to be applied precisely. In contrast, uncertainty in carbon-film thickness was associated with oxygen concentrations several wt% below stoichiometric values. The excerpt also warns that high-attenuation coatings such as gold and platinum are generally unsuitable for quantitative work and that coating choice can influence accuracy. The software correction described requires specifying the coating element and thickness. However, this passage does not discuss take-off-angle dependence, standards and unknowns having different coatings, explicit coating-generated characteristic peaks, or multilayer coating corrections. Those practices therefore cannot be established from this excerpt alone.

The excerpt directly addresses coating effects on low-energy X-ray quantification. It reports that a 5 nm osmium coating attenuates X-rays by approximately 11%, whereas a 15–20 nm carbon coating attenuates them by about 4–6%. Oxygen is particularly affected because its characteristic X-ray has lower energy than those of the other elements. Consequently, uncertainty in coating thickness produces a significant quantitative error: an error of ±5 nm in carbon-coating thickness gives an uncertainty of approximately 1.7% in the measured oxygen concentration. The authors emphasize that attenuation can be corrected if the actual coating thickness is supplied to the software, but fixed or default thickness values can cause non-negligible errors. Osmium is presented as advantageous because its plasma-CVD thickness is reproducible and controllable through coating time, discharge current, and pressure. The passage also notes that coating composition can contribute interfering characteristic radiation: gold is unsuitable for precise carbon analysis because gold’s N-fluorescent X-rays overlap the carbon K line at 0.277 keV. This excerpt does not explicitly discuss take-off-angle dependence, standards and unknowns having different coatings, or multilayer-coating correction procedures.

The excerpt states that conductive or contaminant surface layers can affect low-keV EPMA. The resulting hydrocarbon or carbon films can contribute a carbon X-ray signal; treating this carbon as uniformly distributed in the interaction volume produces an overestimate when it actually occurs in localized contamination spots. Carbon also absorbs X-rays from other elements, so an incorrect carbon estimate propagates into the calculated concentrations of Fe, Si, Ni, and other elements. For quantitative work, the excerpt recommends correcting for the surface film rather than simply ignoring carbon. STRATAGem can compare measured k-ratios with X-ray generation and absorption models, represent one or more layers above the sample, and model carbon either in the substrate or in a surface film. The table illustrates that modeling carbon in the film produced EPMA results close to APT results. At low accelerating voltage, standards should be carefully matched to unknowns, or suitable nonstandard lines should be used, because chemical shifts, self-absorption, cross-section changes, and absorption-edge effects become important. The excerpt directly supports the importance of accounting for carbonaceous surface films in electron-probe analysis. Electron-beam exposure can produce a contamination layer, mainly carbon, from pump oil or hydrocarbons. This layer contributes its own carbon X-ray signal by enhancing C Ka intensity and simultaneously reduces the intensities of other X-ray lines through absorption. The passage therefore indicates that a coating can both generate a characteristic signal and attenuate signals originating from the specimen. It recommends keeping samples clean, storing them under vacuum where possible, using an oil trap, and employing a liquid-nitrogen cold finger or gas jet to prevent or remove contamination. The excerpt does not specifically quantify attenuation as a function of coating thickness or take-off angle, nor does it discuss a formal multilayer correction algorithm. For quantitative EPMA, it emphasizes using strong, stable, reproducible, homogeneous, independently characterized standards and selecting standards similar in composition and structure to the unknown. Such matching is intended to minimize matrix effects and spectral differences, including peak shifts and shape changes. By implication, standards and unknowns should have comparable surface conditions; otherwise, coating-related signal enhancement and absorption can bias quantitative results.

This excerpt provides evidence mainly about carbon contamination during low-keV EPMA, rather than about intentionally applied conductive coatings. It states that carbon may be a real constituent of the Fe-Si minerals and can also interfere with analysis at low accelerating voltage. Electron-beam exposure produces hydrocarbon-related carbon buildup, visible as approximately 2-µm carbon rings, and this contamination can contribute to measured carbon signal and complicate quantitative interpretation. The authors used vacuum cold plates to trap hydrocarbons, plasma cleaning to reduce contamination, and a refrigerant-cooled head where liquid-nitrogen boiling caused vibrations that could destabilize analysis on submicron grains. Because carbon continued to accumulate during measurement, they used time-dependent intensity correction, dividing analyses into multiple subperiods. They also measured background carbon in samples expected to contain none or less than detection level and subtracted that measured background from subsequent analyses. The excerpt does not state that conductive coatings were used, does not describe characteristic X-ray contributions from coating materials beyond carbon contamination, and does not discuss attenuation or absorption of low-energy X-rays as a function of coating thickness or take-off angle. It likewise contains no guidance on matching coating conditions between standards and unknowns or on multilayer coating corrections.

A carbon-coated MgO standard will normally show coating-derived C Kα in every spectrum acquired from its coated surface. Carbonaceous surface films are documented both to produce their own carbon X-rays and to absorb X-rays emitted by the underlying material. Treating surface-film carbon as though it were uniformly distributed through a bulk specimen gives incorrect carbon concentrations and propagates errors into the matrix correction (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).

- The coated MgO remains usable as an **Mg and O standard**, provided coating absorption is canceled by matching or is corrected.

For a planar film of normal thickness *t* and take-off angle θ measured from the specimen surface, substrate X-ray transmission is approximately

**T = exp[−(μ/ρ)ρt/sin θ]**, with attenuation **A = 1 − T**.

## Conclusion

**Yes:** an evaporated carbon film is itself excited by the electron beam and contributes a C Kα peak near 0.277 keV. **For a 10–25 nm film, O Kα is attenuated by a few percent—roughly 2–8% over that thickness range—whereas Mg Kα attenuation is usually well below 1%.** For rigorous standard-based work, matching the coatings remains the safest practice; when standards and unknowns cannot be matched, the known coating should be handled explicitly as a surface layer.

### 1. Carbon peak and carbon analysis

A carbon-coated MgO standard will normally show coating-derived C Kα in every spectrum acquired from its coated surface. Carbonaceous surface films are documented both to produce their own carbon X-rays and to absorb X-rays emitted by the underlying material. Treating surface-film carbon as though it were uniformly distributed through a bulk specimen gives incorrect carbon concentrations and propagates errors into the matrix correction (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).

Consequently:

- The coated MgO remains usable as an **Mg and O standard**, provided coating absorption is canceled by matching or is corrected.
- It is **not a clean bulk-carbon standard**. A thin carbon film does not have the geometry or electron/X-ray generation behavior of a bulk carbon standard.
- Ordinary bulk EDS/EPMA cannot uniquely distinguish carbon in the coating from carbon in the specimen because both contribute at C Kα. Thus, a coated unknown is generally unsuitable for direct intrinsic-carbon determination unless coating thickness is independently known and a validated layered-film model, blank/differential measurement, or another analytical strategy is used.
- Beam-induced hydrocarbon deposition adds a further, time-dependent carbon contribution, so clean vacuum practice, plasma cleaning/cold trapping, and time-dependent checks matter for carbon work (pqac-00000006).

### 2. Approximate attenuation

For a planar film of normal thickness *t* and take-off angle θ measured from the specimen surface, substrate X-ray transmission is approximately

**T = exp[−(μ/ρ)ρt/sin θ]**, with attenuation **A = 1 − T**.

At θ = 35–40°, the X-ray path through the film is about **1.56–1.74 times** its normal thickness. Published EDS calculations report approximately **4–6% attenuation for low-energy O Kα through a 15–20 nm carbon coat**, and emphasize that oxygen is particularly sensitive to uncertainty in coating thickness (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005).

| Carbon thickness (nm) | Effective path, *t*/sin θ (nm), θ = 35–40° | O Kα attenuation at 0.525 keV (%) | Mg Kα attenuation at 1.254 keV (%) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 10 | 15.6–17.4 | ≈2–3 | ≈0.1–0.2 |
| 15 | 23.3–26.2 | ≈4–5 | ≈0.2–0.3 |
| 20 | 31.1–34.9 | ≈5–6 | ≈0.2–0.4 |
| 25 | 38.9–43.6 | ≈6–8 | ≈0.3–0.6 |


*Table: Estimated attenuation by an evaporated carbon coat at a 35–40° take-off angle. O Kα values are anchored to the published 4–6% attenuation for 15–20 nm carbon and scaled by Beer–Lambert optical depth (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005); Mg Kα values are rough coefficient-based estimates and depend on film density and the attenuation database.*

These numbers should be treated as practical estimates, not universal constants. They vary with the actual film mass thickness—density × thickness—carbon-film porosity/contamination, take-off angle, and the attenuation-coefficient database. The **O estimates are literature-anchored**. The **Mg estimates are coefficient-based order-of-magnitude values**; because 1.254-keV Mg Kα is much less strongly absorbed by carbon than 0.525-keV O Kα, its loss through this thickness range should ordinarily be only a few tenths of a percent.

The coating can also alter electron energy and X-ray generation slightly, although for 10–25 nm carbon at conventional SEM/EPMA voltages, absorption is the principal line-specific effect under discussion. Complete multilayer models account for electron scattering/energy loss as well as X-ray absorption and fluorescence (pqac-00000000).

### 3. Coated standard versus uncoated conductive metals

**Preferred metrological practice:** put the same coating material and approximately the same mass thickness on standards and unknowns, preferably coating them together. EPMA teaching guidance explicitly recommends equal coating thickness, commonly around 250 Å (25 nm) for conventional analysis (pqac-00000007). Matching causes most coating effects to cancel in the measured unknown/standard intensity ratio.

If the conductive metal unknowns must remain uncoated, do **not** simply combine their uncoated intensities with an uncorrected coated-MgO standard. The coating suppresses the standard’s O and Mg intensities, especially O. For an uncoated unknown, this makes the corresponding measured k-ratio too large and therefore tends to bias the reported concentration upward—by approximately the coating attenuation before nonlinear matrix-correction effects. For example, 5% suppression of the standard’s O intensity increases the raw O k-ratio by about 1/0.95 − 1 = **5.3%**.

The alternatives, in preferred order, are:

1. **Use an uncoated, conductive standard** appropriate for the relevant element and line, if available and suitably characterized.
2. **Match the coatings**, even though the unknown metal does not require one electrically. This is generally simplest and least model-dependent.
3. **Measure the carbon-film mass thickness and apply a validated coating/multilayer correction** to the coated standard. Armstrong reports that multilayer correction substantially improved analyses with differing carbon coatings, while warning that uncorrected coating differences can produce errors exceeding 5–10% in some cases (pqac-00000000).

For **NIST DTSA-II**, use this third route only if the specific quantification workflow explicitly represents the carbon as a film over the standard and applies that geometry consistently when predicting the standard intensity or k-ratio. Enter carbon as an overlayer with measured thickness/density—not as carbon dissolved in bulk MgO. A generic bulk ZAF/φ(ρz) correction, or merely including C in the fitted composition, is not equivalent to a layered correction. Layered programs can correctly model carbon as a surface film rather than substrate carbon (pqac-00000003).

Because the retrieved literature establishes the validity of multilayer corrections but does not document a particular DTSA-II interface or version-specific command, the correction should be validated experimentally—for example, by comparing coated and uncoated measurements of a conductive reference. If DTSA-II’s workflow cannot explicitly model the asymmetry of a coated standard and uncoated unknown, matching coatings or using an uncoated standard is preferable to an ad hoc intensity correction.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly supports the importance of accounting for carbonaceous surface films in electron-probe analysis. Electron-beam exposure can produce a contamination layer, mainly carbon, from pump oil or hydrocarbons. This layer contributes its own carbon X-ray signal by enhancing C Ka intensity and simultaneously reduces the intensities of other X-ray lines through absorption. The passage therefore indicates that a coating can both generate a characteristic signal and attenuate signals originating from the specimen. It recommends keeping samples clean, storing them under vacuum where possible, using an oil trap, and employing a liquid-nitrogen cold finger or gas jet to prevent or remove contamination. The excerpt does not specifically quantify attenuation as a function of coating thickness or take-off angle, nor does it discuss a formal multilayer correction algorithm. For quantitative EPMA, it emphasizes using strong, stable, reproducible, homogeneous, independently characterized standards and selecting standards similar in composition and structure to the unknown. Such matching is intended to minimize matrix effects and spectral differences, including peak shifts and shape changes. By implication, standards and unknowns should have comparable surface conditions; otherwise, coating-related signal enhancement and absorption can bias quantitative results.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: In SEM-EDS / EPMA microanalysis, MgO (periclase) is used as a standard for Mg and O. If the MgO standard must be carbon-coated for conductivity: (1) does the coating itself add a C K-alpha peak to every spectrum, making a coated sample unusable as a carbon standard or for measuring sample carbon? (2) Roughly how much are O K-alpha (0.525 keV) and Mg K-alpha (1.254 keV) intensities attenuated by a 10-25 nm evaporated carbon coat at a 35-40 degree take-off angle? (3) What is best practice when the standard is coated but the unknowns are uncoated conductive metals - match the coating, or correct for it in software such as NIST DTSA-II?

## Conclusion

**Yes:** an evaporated carbon film is itself excited by the electron beam and contributes a C Kα peak near 0.277 keV. **For a 10–25 nm film, O Kα is attenuated by a few percent—roughly 2–8% over that thickness range—whereas Mg Kα attenuation is usually well below 1%.** For rigorous standard-based work, matching the coatings remains the safest practice; when standards and unknowns cannot be matched, the known coating should be handled explicitly as a surface layer.

### 1. Carbon peak and carbon analysis

A carbon-coated MgO standard will normally show coating-derived C Kα in every spectrum acquired from its coated surface. Carbonaceous surface films are documented both to produce their own carbon X-rays and to absorb X-rays emitted by the underlying material. Treating surface-film carbon as though it were uniformly distributed through a bulk specimen gives incorrect carbon concentrations and propagates errors into the matrix correction (gopon2017ultra‐reducedphasesin pages 6-8, graser2008electronprobemicroanalysis pages 2-3).

Consequently:

- The coated MgO remains usable as an **Mg and O standard**, provided coating absorption is canceled by matching or is corrected.
- It is **not a clean bulk-carbon standard**. A thin carbon film does not have the geometry or electron/X-ray generation behavior of a bulk carbon standard.
- Ordinary bulk EDS/EPMA cannot uniquely distinguish carbon in the coating from carbon in the specimen because both contribute at C Kα. Thus, a coated unknown is generally unsuitable for direct intrinsic-carbon determination unless coating thickness is independently known and a validated layered-film model, blank/differential measurement, or another analytical strategy is used.
- Beam-induced hydrocarbon deposition adds a further, time-dependent carbon contribution, so clean vacuum practice, plasma cleaning/cold trapping, and time-dependent checks matter for carbon work (gopon2017ultra‐reducedphasesin pages 8-9).

### 2. Approximate attenuation

For a planar film of normal thickness *t* and take-off angle θ measured from the specimen surface, substrate X-ray transmission is approximately

**T = exp[−(μ/ρ)ρt/sin θ]**, with attenuation **A = 1 − T**.

At θ = 35–40°, the X-ray path through the film is about **1.56–1.74 times** its normal thickness. Published EDS calculations report approximately **4–6% attenuation for low-energy O Kα through a 15–20 nm carbon coat**, and emphasize that oxygen is particularly sensitive to uncertainty in coating thickness (ohfuji2015edsquantificationof pages 3-5, ohfuji2015edsquantificationof pages 2-3).

| Carbon thickness (nm) | Effective path, *t*/sin θ (nm), θ = 35–40° | O Kα attenuation at 0.525 keV (%) | Mg Kα attenuation at 1.254 keV (%) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 10 | 15.6–17.4 | ≈2–3 | ≈0.1–0.2 |
| 15 | 23.3–26.2 | ≈4–5 | ≈0.2–0.3 |
| 20 | 31.1–34.9 | ≈5–6 | ≈0.2–0.4 |
| 25 | 38.9–43.6 | ≈6–8 | ≈0.3–0.6 |


*Table: Estimated attenuation by an evaporated carbon coat at a 35–40° take-off angle. O Kα values are anchored to the published 4–6% attenuation for 15–20 nm carbon and scaled by Beer–Lambert optical depth (ohfuji2015edsquantificationof pages 3-5, ohfuji2015edsquantificationof pages 2-3); Mg Kα values are rough coefficient-based estimates and depend on film density and the attenuation database.*

These numbers should be treated as practical estimates, not universal constants. They vary with the actual film mass thickness—density × thickness—carbon-film porosity/contamination, take-off angle, and the attenuation-coefficient database. The **O estimates are literature-anchored**. The **Mg estimates are coefficient-based order-of-magnitude values**; because 1.254-keV Mg Kα is much less strongly absorbed by carbon than 0.525-keV O Kα, its loss through this thickness range should ordinarily be only a few tenths of a percent.

The coating can also alter electron energy and X-ray generation slightly, although for 10–25 nm carbon at conventional SEM/EPMA voltages, absorption is the principal line-specific effect under discussion. Complete multilayer models account for electron scattering/energy loss as well as X-ray absorption and fluorescence (armstrong2009useofmultilayer pages 1-2).

### 3. Coated standard versus uncoated conductive metals

**Preferred metrological practice:** put the same coating material and approximately the same mass thickness on standards and unknowns, preferably coating them together. EPMA teaching guidance explicitly recommends equal coating thickness, commonly around 250 Å (25 nm) for conventional analysis (chatterjee2012electronmicroprobeanalysis pages 36-39). Matching causes most coating effects to cancel in the measured unknown/standard intensity ratio.

If the conductive metal unknowns must remain uncoated, do **not** simply combine their uncoated intensities with an uncorrected coated-MgO standard. The coating suppresses the standard’s O and Mg intensities, especially O. For an uncoated unknown, this makes the corresponding measured k-ratio too large and therefore tends to bias the reported concentration upward—by approximately the coating attenuation before nonlinear matrix-correction effects. For example, 5% suppression of the standard’s O intensity increases the raw O k-ratio by about 1/0.95 − 1 = **5.3%**.

The alternatives, in preferred order, are:

1. **Use an uncoated, conductive standard** appropriate for the relevant element and line, if available and suitably characterized.
2. **Match the coatings**, even though the unknown metal does not require one electrically. This is generally simplest and least model-dependent.
3. **Measure the carbon-film mass thickness and apply a validated coating/multilayer correction** to the coated standard. Armstrong reports that multilayer correction substantially improved analyses with differing carbon coatings, while warning that uncorrected coating differences can produce errors exceeding 5–10% in some cases (armstrong2009useofmultilayer pages 1-2).

For **NIST DTSA-II**, use this third route only if the specific quantification workflow explicitly represents the carbon as a film over the standard and applies that geometry consistently when predicting the standard intensity or k-ratio. Enter carbon as an overlayer with measured thickness/density—not as carbon dissolved in bulk MgO. A generic bulk ZAF/φ(ρz) correction, or merely including C in the fitted composition, is not equivalent to a layered correction. Layered programs can correctly model carbon as a surface film rather than substrate carbon (gopon2017ultra‐reducedphasesin pages 6-8).

Because the retrieved literature establishes the validity of multilayer corrections but does not document a particular DTSA-II interface or version-specific command, the correction should be validated experimentally—for example, by comparing coated and uncoated measurements of a conductive reference. If DTSA-II’s workflow cannot explicitly model the asymmetry of a coated standard and uncoated unknown, matching coatings or using an uncoated standard is preferable to an ad hoc intensity correction.

info.query: In SEM-EDS / EPMA microanalysis, MgO (periclase) is used as a standard for Mg and O. If the MgO standard must be carbon-coated for conductivity: (1) does the coating itself add a C K-alpha peak to every spectrum, making a coated sample unusable as a carbon standard or for measuring sample carbon? (2) Roughly how much are O K-alpha (0.525 keV) and Mg K-alpha (1.254 keV) intensities attenuated by a 10-25 nm evaporated carbon coat at a 35-40 degree take-off angle? (3) What is best practice when the standard is coated but the unknowns are uncoated conductive metals - match the coating, or correct for it in software such as NIST DTSA-II?
